section_summary: This section begins with the conclusion of a consular report on the Kwantung Government’s 1933–34 budget, including opium-monopoly revenue and expenditures connected with Japanese activities in Manchuria. Most of the section concerns narcotics regulation, surveillance, prosecutions, clandestine morphine and heroin factories, suspected international smugglers, and the notably light sentences imposed by Dairen courts. It also contains the 1933 South Manchuria Railway Zone opium ordinance and later Treasury intelligence reports on drug factories, shipping routes, opium shops, and opium revenues in Manchuria and southwestern China.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Government budget and opium-monopoly finances
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports on the Kwantung Government’s revenue, expenditures, borrowing, opium-monopoly income, and spending connected with Japanese activities in Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: The report compares the 1931–34 budgets and argues that the Kwantung Government was largely self-supporting when expenditures on South Manchuria Railway policing are treated as extra-territorial. It discusses concealed or separately remitted income from the opium monopoly and details extraordinary appropriations for aviation, salt production, communications, police armament, and aid to the railway company. Vincent concludes that the budget reflects the overlapping functions of the Kwantung Government, Kwantung Army, and South Manchuria Railway Company.

subfiles.title: Letter on movements of suspected narcotics traffickers
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: M. R. Nicholson, United States Treasury Attaché at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Reports the travel and financial activities of Devineau, Shifman, Beerbrayer, Gourevitch, Kapustin, Podliatschuk, and other suspected traffickers.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reports that Japanese police expected Devineau to arrive in Dairen and describes increased travel between Dairen, Kobe, Tientsin, and Shanghai following Shifman’s return. He gives a detailed account of Beerbrayer’s unusual sterling transactions through the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation. The British consul suspected that these transactions were connected with narcotics trafficking and noted Beerbrayer’s appearance in the Eliepoulos disclosures.

subfiles.title: Baori–Takushima narcotics case and Bogdanovsky notebook
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Updates the Bacri–Takushima prosecution and transcribes names and addresses found in Boris Bogdanovsky’s notebook.
subfiles.summary: Vincent reviews the original sentences, the procurator’s appeal, repeated delays in retrial, Bacri’s escape, and Bogdanovsky’s brief arrest on returning to Dairen. Police seized a notebook listing contacts across Harbin, Tientsin, Shanghai, Paris, Berlin, Hamburg, Peiping, and Los Angeles. Vincent observes that several names also appeared on the Department’s alien-suspect list, making the notebook potentially incriminating.

subfiles.title: Regulations for the Control of Opium in the South Manchuria Railway Areas
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits and interprets the new Kwantung ordinance extending opium controls and the monopoly system into the South Manchuria Railway areas.
subfiles.summary: Vincent explains that the regulations, effective May 10, were intended to extend the Kwantung Government Opium Monopoly Bureau’s operations into the railway zone. He compares them with the more detailed Kwantung Leased Territory rules and with the recently promulgated Manchukuo opium law. He interprets the change as technically significant evidence of expanding Japanese jurisdiction following the events of September 1931.

subfiles.title: Kwantung Government Ordinance No. 14: Regulations for the Control of Opium in the South Manchuria Railway Zone
subfiles.to: Residents and officials of the South Manchuria Railway Zone
subfiles.about: Defines the licensing, sale, possession, inspection, and punishment regime for opium in the railway zone.
subfiles.summary: The ordinance prohibits opium smoking except for licensed confirmed adult smokers and reserves raw-opium distribution to the government. It regulates retail dealers, manufacturers, purchase limits, sales records, inspections, poppy cultivation, and disposition of remaining stocks. Violations are punishable by detention or fine, and the ordinance took effect on May 10, 1933.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Baori–Takushima case report to the Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards Dairen despatch No. 41 concerning the Bacri–Takushima case and Bogdanovsky’s seized list.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends the report confidentially for the Commissioner of Narcotics. It highlights both the movements of persons involved in the case and the names and addresses found in Bogdanovsky’s possession.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Vincent’s May 4 letter to the Bureau of Narcotics
subfiles.about: Forwards the confidential letter on Devineau, Shifman, Gourevitch, and other suspected narcotics traffickers.
subfiles.summary: The State Department supplies the Acting Commissioner of Narcotics with a copy of Vincent’s May 4 letter to Nicholson. The document identifies the letter as intelligence on the Far Eastern movements of important traffickers.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Vincent’s May 4 letter to the Commissioner of Customs
subfiles.about: Forwards the May 4 intelligence letter for the Commissioner of Customs.
subfiles.summary: This parallel transmittal sends Vincent’s letter to the customs authorities on a strictly confidential basis. It describes the enclosure as concerning the movements of important narcotics traffickers in the Far East.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of South Manchuria Railway opium regulations
subfiles.about: Forwards Dairen despatch No. 39 and its translated opium-control ordinance to the Commissioner of Narcotics.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends the Dairen report and enclosure for the information of the Commissioner of Narcotics. The subject is regulation of opium traffic in the South Manchuria Railway area.

subfiles.title: The Shirakawa “Benzolin Case”
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the Supreme Court convictions and sentences of ten defendants in the Shirakawa benzoylmorphine-smuggling case.
subfiles.summary: Chief Justice Fujisaki and two associate justices convicted all ten defendants after lower courts had acquitted them. Most were released immediately because pretrial detention counted toward their very short sentences, while Kawai received a stay. Vincent calls the punishments amazingly mild given the smuggling of 5,550 kilograms of narcotics but commends the procurator’s persistence.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Shirakawa retrial report
subfiles.about: Forwards Vincent’s report on the retrial of Shirakawa and nine others.
subfiles.summary: The report is sent for the Commissioner of Narcotics’ information. The transmittal identifies the case as involving the illegal importation of benzolin into Dairen.

subfiles.title: Passport issued to George Israel Tribe
subfiles.about: Notifies Treasury that George Israel Tribe received a new American passport while his Dairen narcotics case awaited retrial.
subfiles.summary: Tribe had been fined by the Dairen District Court in April 1932 for trafficking in narcotics. He told the American consul general at Shanghai that he had lived there since November 1932 and worked as an automobile salesman for a Ford agent.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note concerning Zachary P. Bogart and the Bogdanovsky family
subfiles.about: Cross-references a Harbin despatch connecting Zachary P. Bogart with Boris, Esther, and Naum Bogdanovsky.
subfiles.summary: The note recalls that Boris Bogdanovsky’s notebook contained both international smugglers’ names and that of his Los Angeles brother, Zachary P. Bogart. It also records Bogart’s efforts to help Esther Bogdanovsky and her son Naum obtain United States visas.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of League of Nations report on the Dairen benzoylin case
subfiles.about: Forwards League of Nations document O.C.S. 173 on the final judgment in the 1930 Dairen benzoylmorphine case.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes a discrepancy between the League document and the American consul’s report concerning the date of the Supreme Court decision. It also contrasts the League’s reference to imprisonment with hard labor with the consul’s report that nine defendants were immediately released and the tenth received a stay.

subfiles.title: League of Nations report sent to the American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Sends the consul a copy of League of Nations document O.C.S. 173 on the Shirakawa case.
subfiles.summary: The instruction refers to Vincent’s July 27, 1933 despatch on the Port Arthur Supreme Court sentences. It provides the League’s account of the final judgment for the consul’s information.

subfiles.title: Discovery of Morphine Plant in Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the explosion and discovery of a clandestine morphine plant operated by Mitsuyoshi Torii and associates.
subfiles.summary: The explosion exposed a factory that had operated since June, injured Kihara and Negishi, and led to several arrests or deaths; Yu Chin-yan escaped. Raw materials reportedly came from Tientsin and most finished morphine was sent back there. Vincent emphasizes Torii’s prior conviction and argues that nominal local sentences failed to deter repeated drug manufacture.

subfiles.title: “Two Injured in Explosion”
subfiles.about: Describes the explosion that demolished Torii’s clandestine morphine factory near Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The report says Kihara and Negishi were seriously injured while manufacturing morphine under Torii’s supervision and that a Chinese accomplice named Yu fled. It states that Torii had postponed serving an earlier sentence, earned nearly 70,000 yen from recent production, and sent most of the morphine to Tientsin.

subfiles.title: Eogonine Smuggling Case—Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the attempted smuggling of government-sold eogonine from Dairen to Osaka and the defendants’ eventual sentences.
subfiles.summary: The Kwantung Government sold 500 kilograms of eogonine to Sandai Pharmacy, after which 250 kilograms were packed for illicit shipment to Tamiya in Osaka. Police seized the drug, but judgment was delayed for more than three years and the court imposed still lighter penalties than those requested by the procurator. Vincent cites the case as further evidence that Dairen’s courts did not deter large-scale narcotics trafficking.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the eogonine-smuggling report
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 94 on the seizure of eogonine and the convictions of those implicated.
subfiles.summary: The despatch is supplied in duplicate for the Commissioner of Narcotics. The Department also directs attention to its earlier communication about the Shirakawa retrial because several defendants overlapped.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Dairen morphine-factory report
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 96 and its newspaper enclosure on the discovery of a Dairen morphine factory.
subfiles.summary: The Department sends the materials in duplicate to the Commissioner of Narcotics. It links the discovery with an earlier report on a clandestine morphine factory at Kokusekisho.

subfiles.title: Instruction commending Dairen narcotics reporting
subfiles.about: Commends the consul’s narcotics reports and requests future narcotics despatches in quintuplicate.
subfiles.summary: The Department describes despatches Nos. 94 and 96 as useful and timely. It asks that a copy of the eogonine report be sent to the Treasury Attaché at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Sentence Given in Connection with Morphine Plant in Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports the sentences imposed on five persons connected with Torii’s morphine plant.
subfiles.summary: Judge Takahashi sentenced Torii and Kihara to penal servitude and fined Kuwata, Nakamura, and Liu. All defendants abandoned their right of appeal. Vincent explains that Nakamura and Liu had not appeared in his earlier report because their connections were discovered later.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of morphine-plant sentencing report
subfiles.about: Forwards Dairen despatch No. 102 on sentences for illicit morphine manufacture.
subfiles.summary: The report is sent in duplicate for the confidential information of the Commissioner of Narcotics. It follows the Department’s October communication on the discovery of the factory.

subfiles.title: Activities of Curt Smith
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits correspondence and telegrams documenting the investigation of Curt Smith and his suspected associates in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Vincent encloses his detailed report to Nicholson and the telegrams that initiated and concluded the inquiry. Smith left Dairen for Shanghai on December 8 without further evidence of local activity. Vincent also identifies Vladimir Kapustin and H. Iribuch as persons attracting narcotics-related suspicion.

subfiles.title: Letter detailing the investigation of Curt Smith
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: M. R. Nicholson, United States Treasury Attaché at Shanghai
subfiles.about: Gives a chronological account of Smith’s bills of exchange, warehoused cargo, contacts, and movements in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Vincent traces shipments of dyes, tinsel, artificial fruit, toys, shoes, and spangles through several banks and shipping firms and records which warehouse warrants Smith obtained. He describes Smith’s meetings with Diatlovitsky, Bruno Haube, Sherell, Iribuch, Kapustin, and others. Although the circumstances suggested illicit preparation, Vincent sought guidance on whether police should inspect the cargo and requested fuller background from Nicholson.

subfiles.title: Telegram initiating surveillance of Curt Smith
subfiles.from: Consulate General at Shanghai, relaying M. R. Nicholson
subfiles.about: Requests discreet investigation of Curt Smith’s proposed bank loan, cargo, and Dairen business connections.
subfiles.summary: Nicholson reports that Smith, listed as a narcotics suspect, intended to travel to Dairen and negotiate a loan secured by European cargo. He asks the consul to identify Smith’s contacts and the bank involved without alerting police or attracting attention.

subfiles.title: Telegram explaining the purpose of Curt Smith’s shipments
subfiles.about: Advises against police intervention because Smith’s small shipments were believed to be tests of Japanese import procedures.
subfiles.summary: The telegram praises Vincent’s information but says police interference would complicate wider investigations in Shanghai, New York, and Europe. Authorities believed the shipments contained no contraband and were intended to study customs, warehousing, port, and cargo-handling procedures.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of the Curt Smith investigation
subfiles.about: Forwards despatch No. 111 and its enclosures concerning Curt Smith.
subfiles.summary: The material is sent in duplicate for the Commissioner of Narcotics’ confidential information. Smith is identified as No. 188 on the confidential list of suspected narcotics traffickers.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal concerning narcotics factories in Dairen
subfiles.doc_type: Treasury Department letter with duplicate copy
subfiles.about: Transmits Nicholson’s November 5, 1934 confidential communication on narcotics factories in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department provides two copies of the report received through the Bureau of Customs. The two pages preserve substantially duplicate copies of the same covering letter.

subfiles.title: Report on five alleged narcotics factories in Dairen
subfiles.from: M. R. Nicholson, Treasury Attaché, incorporating a report from Chang Chien
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Reports intelligence gathered by covert agents on five alleged heroin and morphine factories in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Chang Chien states that Sung Hai-shan located five factories while Wang Toh-yuan was arrested by Japanese police. The report supplies alleged factory addresses, proprietors, products, and monthly production estimates, while describing the severe difficulty of communicating under censorship. It further claims extensive smuggling from Dairen into China and requests continued funding for the intelligence network; page 292 repeats part of the poorly reproduced report.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal concerning Greek steamships and narcotics suspects
subfiles.about: Transmits reports on Greek steamships visiting Dairen and persons suspected of narcotics trafficking.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter forwards a Bureau of Customs letter and Nicholson’s April 30 report. It specifically calls attention to M. Podliatschuk, who had already appeared in interdepartmental correspondence.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Customs transmittal of Greek-steamship report
subfiles.from: Edson J. Shamhart, Chief, Division of Enforcement
subfiles.about: Forwards Nicholson’s report on Greek steamships visiting Dairen between January and April 1935.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau of Customs supplies the report for the Commissioner of Narcotics’ information. It identifies Nicholson as the Treasury Attaché at Shanghai and the subject as recent Greek shipping at Dairen.

subfiles.title: Report on Greek steamships and suspected “white cargo” traffic
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Lists Greek vessels calling at Dairen and reports allegations of narcotics shipments and movements of suspected smugglers.
subfiles.summary: A Dairen agent lists six calls by Greek steamships chartered largely for Soviet cargo and alleges that crews carried narcotics or planned to bring Persian opium. The report names local stevedores and records the arrival or departure of Podliatschuk, Mvridis, Tziklidis, Panaidis, and Brinberg. It also alleges plans to organize shipments of “white cargo” from Dairen to Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal concerning drug manufacture and distribution in Dairen
subfiles.about: Transmits a Bureau of Customs report on drug manufacture and distribution in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter forwards the Bureau’s May 25 communication and Nicholson’s April 29 report. The material is supplied in two copies for State Department use.

subfiles.title: Bureau of Customs transmittal of Dairen drug-distribution report
subfiles.from: Edson J. Shamhart, Chief, Division of Enforcement
subfiles.about: Forwards Nicholson’s report on drug manufacture and distribution in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Bureau sends the report for the Commissioner of Narcotics’ information. The enclosure is identified as a Shanghai Treasury Attaché report dated April 29, 1935.

subfiles.title: Drug Manufacture and Distribution in Dairen
subfiles.from: M. R. Nicholson, Treasury Attaché, reporting information from a Manchurian agent
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Surveys alleged narcotics manufacture, pricing, retail distribution, and maritime smuggling centered on Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The agent argues that Dairen became the chief center of morphine and heroin production after Japanese expansion in Manchuria and describes factories disguised as legitimate chemical or medicine works. Government opium dens and brothels allegedly retailed narcotics, while factories in Mukden and Antung supplied additional railway towns. The report estimates large weekly shipments to Chinese ports and overseas destinations, gives wholesale and retail prices, and alleges protection or participation by Japanese officials and steamship crews.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal concerning a discovered Dairen drug factory
subfiles.about: Transmits Nicholson’s April 16 report concerning a drug factory discovered in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department sends two copies of the report to the State Department. The brief covering letter identifies the source as the Treasury Attaché at Shanghai.

subfiles.title: Treasury transmittal of September 1935 narcotics-factory report
subfiles.doc_type: Treasury Department letter with duplicate copy
subfiles.from: Stephen B. Gibbons, Assistant Secretary of the Treasury
subfiles.about: Transmits Nicholson’s September 2 report on narcotics factories in Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Treasury Department forwards two copies of the Shanghai report. Page 304 is a duplicate or carbon of the same covering communication.

subfiles.title: Four newly reported narcotics factories in Dairen
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Identifies four alleged Japanese-operated heroin or morphine factories and their Dairen locations.
subfiles.summary: Nicholson reports information from a Dairen agent who claimed that four newly located factories operated with local police protection. The report names Imahashi, Matsuda, and Tani as operators and says their products were distributed through Dairen, Manchuria, and North China.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of four reports on opium shops, factories, and revenues
subfiles.about: Forwards reports on opium shops in Harbin, Antung, and Dairen; secret Dairen factories; Changchun shops; and the Zunyi opium situation.
subfiles.summary: The covering letter enumerates four reports dated September 5–7, 1935. Together they concern retail establishments, clandestine manufacture, and government opium revenues in Manchuria and Guizhou.

subfiles.title: Leading Opium Shops in Harbin, Antung and Dairen
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Lists major opium establishments in Harbin, Antung, and Dairen and describes their narcotics retailing.
subfiles.summary: The report provides shop names and locations in each of the three cities. It says many large shops furnished beds for opium smokers and also sold morphine, heroin, and narcotic mixtures. Nicholson alleges that this illegal trade operated almost openly with Japanese police protection and absorbed the output of Japanese drug manufacturers.

subfiles.title: Secret Drug Factories in the Suburbs of Dairen
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Reports three cave-based factories near Laohutan and another factory operating as the Paiyodo Pharmacy.
subfiles.summary: The three suburban factories were allegedly run by Kajida, Fujigatashi, and Watanabe and produced about 120 ounces of heroin daily apiece. Their products were said to move through Dairen offices to Qingdao, Longkou, Chefoo, Tientsin, and foreign destinations aboard the Kyodo Maru. A fourth factory, operated by Hoia Jih-seng and an unnamed Japanese partner, allegedly supplied Qingdao.

subfiles.title: Opium Retail Shops in Changchun
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Reports 1935 opium-sale receipts in Changchun and the expansion of licensed retail and smoking shops.
subfiles.summary: Forty shops outside the Japanese concession reportedly collected $745,184 during the first half of 1935, excluding wholesale trade. The report says Manchukuo’s Opium Monopoly Bureau reduced the required deposit for new shops, causing rapid growth in both rural outlets and the number of addicts.

subfiles.title: A Survey of the Opium Situation in Tsunyi
subfiles.to: Commissioner of Customs, Division of Customs Agents
subfiles.about: Surveys Zunyi’s strategic importance, opium revenues and production, taxes, retail shops, and addicted population.
subfiles.summary: The report describes Zunyi as a major commercial and military center linking Guizhou and Sichuan whose political importance rested partly on opium revenue. It presents annual revenue and production figures, identifies the military regimes that controlled the proceeds, and lists numerous taxes and surtaxes on cultivation and trade. It estimates 169 substantial district shops, roughly 1,500 smaller village shops and smoking dens, and at least 175,000 addicts; the report continues beyond page 312.
